newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada govt says will help Canadian Airlines.
newsitem.headline: Canada govt says will help Canadian Airlines.

text.p: Canada's federal government said on Wednesday that it was willing in principle to participate in a rescue plan for Canadian Airlines Corp, a crucial step forward in the carrier's efforts to seal a restructuring package by a 3 a.m. EST deadline.

Canadian Transport Minister David Anderson said the federal government would introduce a fuel tax rebate for the industry allowing carriers, "which have significant losses over a number of years," to claim rebates. In addition, the government would extend repayment of loans owed by Canadian Airlines by 12 to 18 months.
Canadian Airlines President Kevin Benson said fuel tax breaks from the federal government and the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia would represent savings of $26 million (C$35 million).
In addition, the proposed restructuring plan would include a further $26 million (C$35 million) in savings from wage concessions by employees.

But Anderson stressed that federal assistance was contingent upon agreement from all six of the company's unions. Four have backed the deal, but two of the biggest unions -- the Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) and the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE) -- have opposed wage reduction. Federal help also hinges on the participation of the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, major creditors and AMR Corp.
Benson said he thought the conditions could be met, but tough negotiations with the two major unions lay ahead.
"There is a lot of work to do before midnight." He stressed that the deadline was firm.
The company has been racing to reach a restructuring deal and set a 3 a.m. EST deadline for agreement from its unions ahead of a creditors' deadline on Saturday.

British Columbia Premier Glen Clark told reporters that he was reassured by discussions in Dallas earlier in the day with officials of AMR Corp, parent of American Airlines and one-third owner of Canadian Airlines. Canadian is asking AMR to reduce $35.6 million (C$48 million) in computer and management fees Canadian pays to AMR. Clark declined to reveal the substance of those discussions.

Dave Ritchie, president of the International Association of Machinists, which has agreed to the restructuring proposal, said he welcomed the federal government's participation in the rescue effort and expressed growing confidence that the airline would remain viable.
